say: Welcome to Math Inquirers P5! This holiday we play with puzzles that stretch your thinking. Every lesson we notice a pattern, test it and explain why.
Today our numbers grow up to 10 million, and you will find out how long a million seconds really is.
Draw seven boxes for millions down to ones. I turn over one digit card at a time. Write it in a box straight away. No moving it later!
The winner is the number closest to 5 000 000. Think: where does a 4 go? A 9? A 0?
Before any working: how long is a million seconds? An hour, a day, a week, a month or a year? Write your guess in the corner of your whiteboard and do not change it.
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: how many seconds in one minute? In one hour? Multiply, do not add.
Stuck on days: you know the seconds in one day. How many days make close to 1 000 000? Try 10 days first.
If a pair wants more: how long is 10 million seconds? More or less than a school term?

say: “Cards 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8. I want the number closest to 5 000 000. I could start with 5 and make the smallest number after it: 5 012 478. That is 12 478 too big.”

“But I must also look just below the target. Start with 4 and make the biggest number after it: 4 875 210. That is 124 790 too small. I compare the two gaps: 12 478 is smaller, so 5 012 478 wins. I always test both sides.”

“For a digit riddle I use the clue that fixes the most digits first. Rounded to the nearest hundred thousand it is 3 600 000, so it starts 3 5 with a big digit next, or 3 6 with a small digit next. Then I follow the other clues one by one and check every clue at the end.”

do: Ask: “Did you look just below AND just above the target?”
Ask: “Which clue fixes the most digits? Start there.”
Ask: “Estimate first. Is the calculator answer about the right size?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Read the number in groups of three from the right: millions, thousands, ones.”
Hint 2: “Write the two best numbers, one just below and one just above, and find each gap.”
Hint 3: “Put each clue’s digit straight into the place-value chart as you go.”

Ask: “Which clue fixes the most digits? Start there.”
Ask: “Estimate first. Is the calculator answer about the right size?”

Hint 2: “Write the two best numbers, one just below and one just above, and find each gap.”

say: “Siti says a 7-digit number is always bigger than a 6-digit number. Ravi says not if the 6-digit number has bigger digits, like 999 999. Who is right?”
“How did you check that your riddle number in Q3 fits every clue?”
ask: “Siti says a 7-digit number is always bigger than a 6-digit number. Ravi says not if the 6-digit number has bigger digits, like 999 999. Who is right?”

Siti is right. The smallest 7-digit number is 1 000 000 and the biggest 6-digit number is 999 999, which is 1 less. A 7-digit number has a millions digit that is at least 1, and that alone beats every 6-digit number, whatever its digits are.

say: “Today you read numbers up to 10 million, tested both sides of a target, followed clues to a single answer and used estimation and brackets. That is how inquirers work with big numbers.”
“Do the exit ticket on your own, then show me.”

p5l1-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Read, write and compare numbers up to 10 million; solve digit-card and digit-riddle puzzles with place value (testing the best number just below AND just above a target); estimate to check large calculations; and use the order of operations and brackets to hit target numbers. Thinking strategies taught today: TEST BOTH SIDES of a target, USE THE CLUES IN ORDER and check every clue, ESTIMATE by rounding, and WRITE THE RANGE FIRST before a "find all". Materials: Digit cards 0 to 9 (one set per child), a 7-column place-value mat (M, HTh, TTh, Th, H, T, O), mini whiteboards, a calculator for the explore (every child needs one; a phone calculator is fine), workbook. Online: children cut out paper digit cards and draw a 7-box mat before the lesson and use them in the lesson (nothing is held up to the camera); the tutor writes on the slides; pairs use breakout rooms for the explore and page 1. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5 (one check for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6.5 to 12.5 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 12.5 to 26.5 (pair work 6 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 26.5 to 37.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 37.5 to 42, workbook page 1 42 to 56.5 (the questions without a star; after question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 56.5 to 60.5, short teaching before page 2 60.5 to 63.5, workbook page 2 63.5 to 71.5 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 71.5 to 74.5, talk time 74.5 to 80 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 80 to 84.5, reflection 84.5 to 87 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 87 to 88, and the buffer 88 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." SPINE: Today's tool is Guess and check. Guess, check, adjust using how far off you were; stop when every condition holds. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p5l1-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE check for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three (face to face, you may glance at papers held low as you walk round; online, nothing is held up to the camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: Starting with 7, the best is 7369 (369 above 7000). Starting with 6, the best is 6973 (27 below 7000). 6973 is closer, and it is the closest of all 24 numbers. A child who only tries numbers that start with 7 misses it: testing BOTH sides of a target is today's idea. Any honest try is a good start.; Q2: (4 + 6) × 5 − 3 = 47. The other single pairs give 16 or 31 (and so does no bracket at all). Brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4.5 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: children say the answers together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE check for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l1-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 9.5. Million Maker. Children draw seven boxes (M, HTh, TTh, Th, H, T, O) on a whiteboard. Shuffle digit cards 0 to 9 and turn over one at a time (online: read the digit aloud; nothing is held up to the camera). After EACH card, children write it in one empty box at once and cannot move it. After seven cards, each child reads their number aloud; the one closest to 5 000 000 wins. Play ONE round only (the clock has room for one). Click to show the thinking question. Talk: "A 4 or a 5 belongs in the millions box: they are next to the target. After a 4, you want BIG digits next (4 9 8 …). After a 5, you want SMALL digits next (5 0 1 …)." Listen for children who say "it depends whether I start with 4 or 5". That is today's big idea: test both sides of a target.

p5l1-warm2.note: Minutes 9.5 to 12.5. Read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click to show. 1) Watch for 340 006: the zeros hold the hundred thousands, thousands, hundreds and tens places. 2) The 7 is in the hundred thousands place. 3) Dividing by 1000 moves every digit three places to the right. 4) The hundreds digit is 5, so round up: 849 thousands becomes 850 thousands. If you are short of time, skip question 4.

p5l1-explore1.note: Minutes 12.5 to 26.5 (the whole explore; this slide 12.5 to 22.5). Pairs. Everybody writes a guess first and does not change it (most children guess a week, a month or a year). Let them work with pencil first; allow a calculator only for checking (before the lesson, confirm that every child has one; a phone calculator is fine). Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): how long is 10 million seconds? More or less than a school term? PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 22.5 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: 10 million seconds is about 116 days, nearly 4 months (10 times as long). A billion seconds is about 11 574 days, which is about 32 years: 1 000 000 000 ÷ 86 400 = 11 574.07 days; 11 574 ÷ 365 is about 31.7 years. A billion is a thousand millions, so 1000 × 11.6 days.

p5l1-explore2.note: Minutes 22.5 to 26.5. Pencils down: gather the pairs. Collect the guesses first: a show of hands for hour, day, week, month, year. Answers: 1) 60 × 60 = 3600 seconds in an hour, 3600 × 24 = 86 400 seconds in a day. 2) 10 days = 864 000 s (not enough), 11 days = 950 400 s, 12 days = 1 036 800 s (too many), so a million seconds is between 11 and 12 days: about 11 and a half days. 3) (Go further what-if, not asked together) 10 million seconds is about 116 days, nearly 4 months (10 times as long). Ask: "Did you multiply or add? Why is multiplying faster?" and "How did you get close without dividing exactly?" (try 10 days, then add a day at a time). Point out the strategy: estimate, then test numbers either side. That links to the digit puzzles next. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): 10 million seconds is about 116 days, nearly 4 months (10 times as long). A billion seconds is about 11 574 days, which is about 32 years: 1 000 000 000 ÷ 86 400 = 11 574.07 days; 11 574 ÷ 365 is about 31.7 years. A billion is a thousand millions, so 1000 × 11.6 days.

p5l1-teach1.note: Minutes 26.5 to 29. Teach. Build 4 053 000 on the place-value mat. Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "The space after every three digits from the right is a comma in words: four million, fifty-three thousand. The 0 in the hundred thousands place still has to be written: it holds the place." Step 3 is the trap: the DIGIT in the thousands place is 3, but the number has 4053 thousands altogether (4 million is 4000 thousands, plus 53 thousands). Ask: "How many hundreds make 4 053 000?" (40 530).

p5l1-try1.note: Minutes 29 to 30. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. a) Watch for 6 205 30 or 6 250 030: thirty is 0 hundreds, 3 tens, 0 ones. b) The 9 is in the ten thousands place. (Two items only; if time allows ask: how many hundreds make 2 400 000? 24 000.)

p5l1-we1.note: Minutes 30 to 32.5. Test both sides: today's main strategy. Ask first: "Which card goes first?" Some children say only 5. Click step 1, then ask "Are we sure? What about just below?" Click step 2. Think-aloud: "After a 5 I want the number as SMALL as possible, so the next digits go up: 0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 8. After a 4 I want it as BIG as possible, so the digits go down: 8, 7, 5, 2, 1, 0. Then I compare the gaps by subtracting." Point out that this time the number just above wins, but on the worksheet it may be the other way: always test both.

p5l1-try2.note: Minutes 32.5 to 34. Whiteboards. a) The ones digit must be odd: keep the 1 for the end, then the rest as big as possible. b) The ones digit must be even: use the smallest even digit that leaves the front small, 8 at the end gives 1 346 798 (ending in 4 gives 1 367 894, ending in 6 gives 1 347 896, both bigger). (Two items only.)

p5l1-we2.note: Minutes 34 to 36.5. Use the clues in order: start with the clue that fixes the most digits. Click order: the digits appear one by one (3, 5, 9, 4, 2, 0, 8), then the two clue notes, then the answer. Talk through the digits as they appear. Think-aloud: "Rounded to the nearest hundred thousand it is 3 600 000, so it is between 3 550 000 and 3 649 999. Either it starts 3 5 and the next digit is 5 or more, or it starts 3 6 and the next digit is 4 or less. Clue 2: 5 + 4 = 9, and 9 is 5 or more, good. 6 + 4 = 10 is not a digit. So 3 5 9. Thousands: 9 − 5 = 4. Hundreds: half of 4 is 2. Tens: 0. So far 3 + 5 + 9 + 4 + 2 + 0 = 23, and 31 − 23 = 8." Then CHECK every clue: 3 594 208 rounds to 3 600 000; all digits different; total 31. The workbook riddle uses the same idea with different clues: do not give it away.

p5l1-key.note: Minutes 36.5 to 37.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Leaving out zeros that hold a place (340 006 for 3 040 006), or mixing up the value of a digit (3000) with how many thousands a number has (4053). (2) Looking only on one side of the target, for example trying only numbers that start with 6 for "closest to 6 000 000". (3) Working from left to right and ignoring the order of operations (6 + 4 × 5 read as 50 instead of 26).

p5l1-break.note: Minutes 37.5 to 42. 4.5 minutes. Online: children stand back from the camera. Ask: "Where is 1 million? Why is it so close to the floor?" (it is only one tenth of the way up).

p5l1-ws1.note: Minutes 42 to 56.5. Walk around. Q3: ask "Which clue fixes the most digits?" (clue 2, the rounding clue). Parts (a), (b), (c) take the riddle one clue at a time; the full six-clue riddle without steps is not asked. (Testing just below AND just above a target is on the Think harder page, A4.) Q1 is take-home (starred): it repeats the quick questions. The check-together slide has its answers for you, but do not explain Q1 in class. Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 3 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q2 (a) (b) and Q3 (a) (b) (c); Q1 is take-home. Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l1-ws1ans.note: Minutes 56.5 to 60.5. One pair explains Q3, the heaviest question; click through the rest (Q1 is take-home). Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q2b: the ones digit must be even; try each even ending with the rest as small as possible: ending 0 gives 2 356 890, ending 2 gives 3 056 892, ending 6 gives 2 035 896, ending 8 gives 2 035 698. The smallest is 2 035 698 Q3: rounding gives 7 2 (then 5 or more) or 7 3 (then 4 or less); 2 + 3 = 5 works, 3 + 3 = 6 does not. Then 5 − 2 = 3, 6, 0, and 32 − 23 = 9.

p5l1-teachest.note: Minutes 60.5 to 62. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Ask first: "Without working it out, is 2 417 336 too big, too small or about right?" Think-aloud: "6 thousand times 4 tens is 24 ten-thousands, 240 000. Mei's answer is over 2 million: way too big." Stress that an estimate cannot prove an answer is RIGHT, only that it COULD be right; it can prove an answer is wrong.

p5l1-teachbrackets.note: Minutes 62 to 63.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Children work out each line on whiteboards before you click. Think-aloud for row 2: "The brackets say add first: 12. Then 12 × 4 = 48, then 48 − 3 = 45." Ask: "Which answer is biggest? Why does (7 + 5) × 4 grow so much?" (the 7 + 5 is multiplied by 4 instead of only the 5).

p5l1-ws2.note: Minutes 63.5 to 71.5. Children work alone on Q4 and Q5 (a) (b); Q5 (c) and Q6 are take-home (starred in the workbook). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who still work from left to right in Q5. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q4 and Q5 (a) (b), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 71.5 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l1-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71.5 to 74.5. One child explains Q5; click through the rest (Q5 (c) and Q6 are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click after a child explains. Q4b: 3 000 000 ÷ 50 = 60 000, so 6259 is 10 times too small (real answer 62 594). Q4c: 2 300 000 + 4 000 000 = 6 300 000 (real answer 6 333 332). Q5c: 1 000 000 ÷ 500 = 2000, × 2 = 4000. Q6: 2 499 499 rounds down to 2 499 000 and 2 500 500 rounds up to 2 501 000; the range is 2 499 500 to 2 500 499. (Think harder A3 adds: the digits add up to 9, find ALL: 2 500 002, 2 500 011, 2 500 020, 2 500 101, 2 500 110, 2 500 200.)

p5l1-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) 7 numbers: 1 000 001, 1 000 010, 1 000 100, 1 001 000, 1 010 000, 1 100 000 and 2 000 000. A2) (2 + 3) × 4 + 5 = 25 and 2 + 3 × (4 + 5) = 29. (29 is the biggest you can make with one pair.) A3) Range: 2 499 500 to 2 500 499. Six numbers: 2 500 002, 2 500 011, 2 500 020, 2 500 101, 2 500 110, 2 500 200. None below 2 500 000: 2 499 5__ already has digits adding to at least 29. A4) 6 987 521 (12 479 below 7 000 000). The best number above is 7 125 689, which is 125 689 away.

p5l1-stretch2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) 7 numbers: 1 000 001, 1 000 010, 1 000 100, 1 001 000, 1 010 000, 1 100 000 and 2 000 000. A2) (2 + 3) × 4 + 5 = 25 and 2 + 3 × (4 + 5) = 29. (29 is the biggest you can make with one pair.) A3) Range: 2 499 500 to 2 500 499. Six numbers: 2 500 002, 2 500 011, 2 500 020, 2 500 101, 2 500 110, 2 500 200. None below 2 500 000: 2 499 5__ already has digits adding to at least 29. A4) 6 987 521 (12 479 below 7 000 000). The best number above is 7 125 689, which is 125 689 away.

p5l1-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 231: (1 + 2) × (3 + 4) × (5 + 6) = 3 × 7 × 11. With no brackets it is only 33. B2) 6 953 487. Seven different digits adding to 42 must be 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 (the biggest seven digits add to exactly 42), so there is no 0. The number is between 6 950 000 and 7 049 999, so it starts 6 9 with 5, 7 or 8 next; the smallest is 6 95 then 3, 4, 8, 7 (it must end in an odd digit). B3) 2893. 9 × 1 + 90 × 2 + 900 × 3 + 4 = 9 + 180 + 2700 + 4. Go further: 5 888 896 (9 × 1 + 90 × 2 + 900 × 3 + 9000 × 4 + 90 000 × 5 + 900 000 × 6 + 7 = 9 + 180 + 2700 + 36 000 + 450 000 + 5 400 000 + 7). Make up your own (printed under Go further): Write your own 7-digit number riddle with three clues. Swap with a partner and solve each other’s riddles. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l1-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 231: (1 + 2) × (3 + 4) × (5 + 6) = 3 × 7 × 11. With no brackets it is only 33. 2) 6 953 487. The seven digits must be 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, because the biggest seven different digits add to exactly 42. The number is between 6 950 000 and 7 049 999; 7 0… needs a 0, so it starts 6 9 then 5, 7 or 8. The smallest: 6 95, then 3, 4, 8, 7 so that it ends in an odd digit.

p5l1-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: E1: "Which makes a number grow faster, adding or multiplying? So which signs should go inside the brackets?" B2: "Which numbers round to 7 000 000? Can the number start 7 0 if it has no 0? What do the biggest seven digits add up to?" Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l1-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: test a few placements first: 1 + 2 × (3 + 4) × 5 + 6 = 77; (1 + 2) × 3 + 4 × (5 + 6) = 53; then all three additions in brackets give 231, the biggest. B2: 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 42 exactly, so there is no room for 0, 1 or 2. After 6 95, the digits 3, 4, 7, 8 are left; 6 953 478 is even, so the smallest odd one is 6 953 487. Check every clue.

p5l1-talk.note: Minutes 74.5 to 80. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: Siti is right. The smallest 7-digit number is 1 000 000 and the biggest 6-digit number is 999 999, which is 1 less. The millions digit of a 7-digit number is at least 1, and that alone beats every 6-digit number. Second question only if time: "How did you check that your riddle number in Q3 fits every clue?" (we went back to Clue 1 and tested each clue in turn). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l1-exit.note: Minutes 80 to 84.5. Answers: (a) 400 000. (b) (5 + 3) × 8 − 2 = 62. (Without brackets it is 27; 5 + 3 × (8 − 2) = 23.) Extension: use the digit cards 0 to 9, each at most once, to make the 7-digit number closest to 5 000 000 (5 012 346 is 12 346 away; 4 987 653 is 12 347 away, so 5 012 346 wins by 1).

p5l1-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 84.5 to 87. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 87 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
